key_concepts: [url]Blender Tutorial: Geometry Nodes for Beginners - Part 1^^https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aO0eUnu0hO0[/url]
Blender tutorial showing how to use Geometry Nodes to create sugar coated candy.

content: Geometry Nodes is like programming, letting you perform actions based on rules you define.

With a brand new scene opened up, go to the Geometry Nodes tab. This will change the interface, showing the 3D Viewport, Spreadsheet, and Geometry Node Editor (Image 1). We won't be using the Spreadsheet so remove this editor (Image 2). In the Geometry Node Editor click [k]New[/k] and it will create a new Geometry Node Modifier for the mesh (Image 3).

image.caption: Image 1 - Opening a new scene and going to the Geometry Nodes tab to see the 3D Viewport, Spreadsheet, and Geometry Node Editor
Image 2 - Removing the Spreadsheet editor
Image 3 - Clicking New in the Geometry Node Editor to create a new Geometry Node Modifier for the mesh

content: Because Geometry Nodes is a modifier, the order matters. Modifiers are applied top-to-bottom. This of Geometry Nodes as post-processing for meshes. In the Geometry Node Editor on the left we can see Geometry Input, which is the mesh, which feeds to the output, which is what is displayed on-screen (Image 4). Anything placed in between those two nodes will affect the output. For example, add a [k]Transform Node[/k] to the editor and update the values; you will see the mesh display change, but in Edit Mode the mesh vertices stay the same (Image 5).

image.caption: Image 4 - Seeing the Geometry Input node feeding to the output node in the Geometry Node Editor
Image 5 - Adding a Transform Node to the editor and updating the values to see the mesh display change while the vertices stay the same in Edit Mode

content: In our project, we want to scatter sugar crystals on a candy, so the node we will use is a [k]Distribute Points on Faces Node[/k]. Add this node to the editor, and you will see the display change; it has taken out mesh and converted it to random points distributed where the faces were (Image 6). Increasing or decreasing the Density will change how many points are displayed.

image.caption: Image 6 - Adding a Distribute Points on Faces Node to the editor and seeing the mesh converted to random points distributed where the faces were

content: Points don't have anything to render, they just hold data. If you were to try to render the mesh right now nothing would display. We want to render the cube mesh and something at those random points. To do that we need a [k]Join Geometry Node[/k] (Image 7). This will join the point data with the mesh data so they both get sent to the output.

image.caption: Image 7 - Adding a Join Geometry Node to join the point data with the mesh data so both get sent to the output

content: Even though we have combined the geometry, nothing will render at those points; we need to supply data for what will be displayed there. We need to add an [k]Instance on Points[/k] node (Image 8). We will see the points disappear from the 3D Viewport, since we haven't identified what instances will be at those points.

image.caption: Image 8 - Adding an Instance on Points node to supply data for what will be displayed at the points

content: If you click on another object that doesn't have the same Geometry Nodes Modifier, the nodes in the editor will disappear. You can click the Pin icon to pin the Geometry Nodes you are working on in the editor.

section.header: Referencing another object in the nodes
content: Add another cube to the scene, [k]S,0.1[/k] to scale it down, and rename it 'sugar.crystal' (Image 9). In order to make it available as a node, grab it from the Outliner and drag it into the Geometry Node Editor (Image 10). Connect the [k]Object Info Node's[/k] Geometry output to the [k]Instance on Points Node's[/k] Instance input (Image 11). The output will look strange; select the sugar.crystal mesh and [k]Ctrl-A,S[/k] to apply the scale and that will fix it (Image 12).

image.caption: Image 9 - Adding another cube to the scene, scaling it down and renaming it 'sugar.crystal'
Image 10 - Grabbing the sugar.crystal mesh from the Outliner and dragging it into the Geometry Node Editor
Image 11 - Connecting the Object Info Node's Geometry output to the Instance on Points Node's Instance input
Image 12 - Selecting the sugar.crystal mesh and applying the scale to fix the strange output

content: We want to add rotation to the sugar crystals, but we want it to be random. Add a [k]Random Value Node[/k], set its Data Type to Vector, and connect its Value output to the [k]Instance on Points Node's[/k] Rotation input (Image 13). The Min and Max fields unit of measurement is radians; 180 degrees is pi radians, so if you type 'pi' into the Max field, Blender will convert it to 3.142 (Image 14). We want the random rotation to be between 0 and 360 degrees. 360 degrees is 2pi, which is called 'tau'. Type 'tau' into the Max field (Image 15).

image.caption: Image 13 - Adding a Random Value Node, setting its Data Type to Vector and connecting its Value output to the Instance on Points Node's Rotation input
Image 14 - Typing 'pi' into the Max field to set the maximum rotation to 180 degrees in radians
Image 15 - Typing 'tau' into the Max field to set the random rotation range to 0 to 360 degrees

content: We also want to randomize the scale, so we need another [k]Random Value Node[/k]. [k]Ctrl-C[/k], [k]Ctrl-V[/k] to duplicate the first one, and connect it to the [k]Instance on Points Node's[/k] Scale input (Image 16). This is distorting the scale on all axes, so some of the shapes are no longer cubes. We want to scale to be uniform on all axes. Change the Data Type to Float to fix this (Image 17). We still have a problem, with the Min set to 0, there are some cubes that are present in memory, but not rendering. Increase the Min to fix this (Image 18).

image.caption: Image 16 - Duplicating the Random Value Node and connecting it to the Instance on Points Node's Scale input to randomize the scale
Image 17 - Changing the Data Type to Float to make the scale uniform on all axes
Image 18 - Increasing the Min value to fix cubes that are present in memory but not rendering

key_concepts: [url]Blender Tutorial: Geometry Nodes for Beginners - Part 2^^https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V10GBrmYIDM[/url]
Blender tutorial showing how to use Geometry Nodes to create sugar coated candy.

content: Geometry Nodes use many variables, from scale, density, rotation, or transformation. These variables are available in the Geometry Node Editor, but it would be convenient if they were accessible somewhere else. We can do that by dragging an input, such as the [k]Distribute Points on Faces Node[/k] Density input to an empty output on the [k]Group Input Node[/k] (Image 1). This will expose the Density value in the Modifier Properties tab on the right (Image 2). Another set of variables that should be exposed are the scale Min and Max values. They show up as 'Min' and 'Max', but that doesn't tell us what values they adjust. We will want to change the names. [k]LMB[/k] the [k]Group Input Node[/k] and [k]N[/k] to bring up the Sidebar on the right (Image 3). Under [k]Group Sockets[/k] you can change the name of the exposed variables (Image 4).

image.caption: Image 1 - Dragging the Distribute Points on Faces Node Density input to an empty output on the Group Input Node to expose it
Image 2 - Seeing the Density value now accessible in the Modifier Properties tab on the right
Image 3 - Clicking the Group Input Node and pressing N to bring up the Sidebar on the right
Image 4 - Changing the names of the exposed variables under Group Sockets

content: If we haven't changed the object's scale since we started, then our sugar candy is 2m tall. This needs to be updated to real-world scale, sinc eit will affect interactions with other meshes that may use different scale, and affect the depth of field when using our camera. Reduce the size from 2m to 2cm; [k]S,0.01[/k] to both the candy and the sugar crystal (Image 5). If you lose sight of the sugar crystal you can [k]Alt-G[/k] to snap it back to the World Origin. [k]Ctrl-A,S[/k] to apply the scale for both objects (Image 6).

image.caption: Image 5 - Reducing the size of both the candy and the sugar crystal from 2m to 2cm to update to real-world scale
Image 6 - Applying the scale for both objects

section.header: Why Object Scale Impacts Point Density
content: After applying the scale, many of the scattered sugar crystals disappeared. That is because since we decreased the candy's size, it takes up less volume in the world, which gives less surface area for those scattered instances to stick. To bring up the number of crystals that appear, we need to increase the Density (Image 7).

image.caption: Image 7 - Increasing the Density to bring back the scattered sugar crystals that disappeared after applying the scale

content: Increasing the Density value by 1000 only added one more visible sugar crystal. We would need to increase the Density exponentially in order to make a difference, but guessing how much to increase it by is not helpful. Add a [k]Multiply Node[/k] to the editor, and set its value to 10,000 (Image 8). This will multiply the value entered into the Modifier Properties tab times 10,000, which will put the Density value on a scale that will make it easier to see in the Viewport (Image 9).

image.caption: Image 8 - Adding a Multiply Node set to 10,000 to make the Density value easier to work with
Image 9 - Seeing the Density value on a more manageable scale in the Viewport

content: The larger and more complex your geometry nodes become, the harder it becomes to follow what each node is doing. Blender comes with a Node Wrangler add-on. Enable it by going to [k]Edit > Preferences[/k] and finding it under Add-ons (Image 10). In the Geometry Nodes Editor, you can select multiple nodes and [k]Shift-P[/k] to group them in a frame (Image 11). With the frame selected, [k]N[/k] to open the Sidebar and under the Node tab, add a Label to the frame (Image 12).

image.caption: Image 10 - Enabling the Node Wrangler add-on by going to Edit > Preferences and finding it under Add-ons
Image 11 - Selecting multiple nodes and grouping them in a frame
Image 12 - Opening the Sidebar with the frame selected and adding a Label under the Node tab

content: Let's start making the cube look like a candy. In Object Mode, [k]Ctrl-1[/k] to add a Subdivision Surface Modifier (Image 13). The surface scattering is wrong because the Geometry Nodes Modifier is being applied before the Subdivision Surface Modifier; move the Subdivision Surface Modifier to the first position (Image 14). Increase the levels to 3 in the Subdivision Surface Modifier (Image 15).

image.caption: Image 13 - Going to Object Mode and adding a Subdivision Surface Modifier
Image 14 - Moving the Subdivision Surface Modifier to the first position to fix the incorrect surface scattering
Image 15 - Increasing the levels to 3 in the Subdivision Surface Modifier

content: Add a Loop Cut to the cube and bring it down in the z-axis to flatten the bottom (Image 16). Scale in the top (Image 17). For the sugar crystals themselves, we don't want them to have such sharp edges; we want some blunt edges that will catch the light. Select the crystal's edges and [k]Ctrl-B[/k] to bevel them, and see the affect this has on the candy (Image 18).

image.caption: Image 16 - Adding a Loop Cut to the cube and bringing it down in the z-axis to flatten the bottom
Image 17 - Scaling in the top
Image 18 - Selecting the crystal's edges, beveling them and seeing the effect on the candy

content: If we look closely, we will see sometimes crystals on the candy's surface overlapping each other (Image 19). This is due to the randomness of the placement. We need more control over how the instances are distributed, so change the Distribution Method to Poisson Disk (Image 20). Making this change removed the [k]Multiply Node[/k] connection; re-connect the [k]Multiply Node's[/k] output to the Density Max input (Image 21). To mitigate the overlap, we need to increase the Distance Min value; this will set a minimum distance between points. Add a new [k]Multiply Node[/k] set to 0.001 and expose the Distance Min in the Modifier Properties to make it easier to set (Image 22).

image.caption: Image 19 - Looking closely and seeing crystals on the candy's surface overlapping each other
Image 20 - Changing the Distribution Method to Poisson Disk to gain more control over instance placement
Image 21 - Re-connecting the Multiply Node's output to the Density Max input after the Distribution Method change removed it
Image 22 - Adding a new Multiply Node set to 0.001 and exposing the Distance Min in the Modifier Properties to set a minimum distance between points

content: Add a material, position the camera, and move the light closer.

image.caption: Image 23 - Final render
